Banca d’Italia · 13 November 2026

How much cash does a BTP trade need at rollover?

Hedge funds moved from lending cash against Italian government bonds to borrowing about €37 billion net by October 2026. A fund can hedge the price of a bond and still need cash tomorrow. What would let it keep the position open?

Observed BTP liquidity on MTS in 2026
Monthly averageBTP turnover (€bn per day)Quoted BTP depth (€bn)Bid–ask spread (bp)
April19.3926.8711.88
September60.2637.285.34
October23.5323.1810.32

Financial Stability Report, Figure 1.6a. Depth measures quantities quoted on the bid and ask sides. The spread measures the cost of crossing between quotes. These cash-market observations do not measure repo haircuts.

How much can the fund borrow against the same bonds?

Suppose a fund pledges bonds worth €100 million, borrows €98 million and must refinance that principal tomorrow. A lender accepting a 2% haircut advances 98% of the current market value. At renewal, the cash the fund must find elsewhere equals the old principal less the amount the lender will now advance. Assume the position size stays fixed and ignore interest, fees and any cash received from a hedge.

Illustrative renewal of a €98 million repo
Change at renewalCollateral value (€m)HaircutCash available (€m)Cash to find (€m)
Original terms1002%98.000.00
Larger haircut1005%95.003.00
Lower bond price972%95.062.94
Both changes975%92.155.85

New cash advance = collateral value × (1 − haircut). The scenarios are illustrative. The Bank reports no common haircut for all funds; its €37 billion figure is net borrowing across covered transactions and cannot be scaled by these hypothetical haircuts to infer a system-wide call.

Test a different rollover

Start with €100 million of bonds and €98 million due tomorrow. Change the lender’s haircut and the fall in the bond price since the original loan.

Cash to find at rollover
Loss on the bonds before hedging

When can the financing gap become selling pressure?

In the combined case, the bond has lost €3 million in market value, but the cash needed to roll the repo is €5.85 million. Solvency depends on the fund’s other assets, liabilities and hedges. Settlement depends on how much unrestricted cash or other eligible collateral it can deliver by the deadline. An offsetting futures gain helps only to the extent that cash is accessible at the right time. To assess selling pressure, check both the repo terms available at rollover and the bids a fund could obtain for the bond. Thin bids matter most when the fund has a cash shortfall to meet.

What would support the forced-sale explanation?

In April 2025 and March 2026, hedge funds reduced their repo borrowing more than other participants as the return-to-volatility profile of Italian government bonds worsened. The reductions were short-lived. To test a future episode, align dealer-level repo renewals, changes in haircuts and variation-margin deadlines with BTP depth and the price impact of a €50 million order (Figure 1.6b). Funding withdrawals preceding broad sales and falling depth would support the mechanism. A widening bid–ask spread while borrowing is rolled at stable terms would weaken that interpretation. Concentration among dealers matters because a fund that loses its lender needs another one ready on the same day.

What the November evidence can establish

October turnover fell from an unusually active September, and the Bank still judged market conditions orderly. Monthly averages cannot identify who sold first. Its repo data cover a non-EU hedge fund only when it trades with an EU counterparty. They do not show the complete funding book, unrestricted cash or hedge of any one fund.

Sources
  • Banca d’Italia. Financial Stability Report No. 2, Figure 1.6 and hedge fund repo box, printed pp. 14–16. 13 November 2026.
  • Banca d’Italia. Data for charts, chapter 1 workbook, sheet “Fig. 1.6”. Monthly cash-market observations.

Czech National Bank · 5–13 November 2026

Why did the CNB raise its inflation forecast while cutting its growth forecast?

The CNB’s autumn forecast raised the 2027 inflation rate by 0.7 percentage points and lowered GDP growth by 0.2 points. The largest inflation revision came from administered prices. The Board’s 25 basis point hike addressed the risk that the shock would spread into other prices.

CNB forecasts for calendar 2027
Annual indicatorSummerAutumnRevision (pp)
Consumer price inflation2.5%3.2%+0.7
Administered price inflation2.4%5.6%+3.2
Core inflation2.5%2.9%+0.4
Real GDP growth2.7%2.5%−0.2
Three-month PRIBOR3.9%4.1%+0.2

Autumn report, pp. 6 and 17. Summer values are reconstructed at the report’s precision by subtracting each published revision. The component inflation rates have different weights in headline CPI. Their revisions cannot be added.

Which part of the shock could monetary policy affect?

Stronger spending can lift both prices and output. Higher production costs can lift prices while reducing output. The Czech revisions fit the second pattern, but several things changed between forecasts. The CNB cites more expensive electricity and gas and a postponed abolition of broadcasting licence fees. Fading relief from the transfer of a renewable-energy fee to the government budget also raises early-2027 annual inflation. Differences in timing can move measured inflation without a new burst of household demand.

Demand nevertheless matters for persistence. The Bank identified tight labour markets, rapid wage growth, robust credit and fiscal support. These make it easier for costs to pass into wages and other prices. A check on that view would use services inflation, unit labour costs and lending alongside actual retail energy tariffs. If administered prices rise as projected while wage pressure and services inflation ease, the evidence for a lasting second round weakens. If weaker investment and consumption accompany tighter long-term financing, the same energy disruption could eventually deliver less inflation than the baseline.

Did policy become looser in real terms?

A borrower’s expected real cost depends on inflation over the life of the loan. The mean of three-month nominal rates during 2027 and average 2027 CPI inflation describe different contracts and horizons. Subtracting the two gives no matched ex-ante real rate. The CNB instead publishes a model-based index combining deviations of the ex-ante real rate and the real exchange rate from their equilibrium levels (Chart 4.13). Negative values mean tighter conditions.

In that index, the reading moves from −0.054 in 2026 Q3 to a projected −0.153 in 2027 Q1. Over the same interval the interest-rate contribution moves from −0.026 to −0.125; the exchange-rate contribution remains close to −0.03. The model therefore implies that most of the additional restraint comes through interest rates. These are index units, not measured real borrowing rates or basis points of policy tightening. This interpretation can be checked against lending rates and spending by borrowers exposed to repricing.

Where did the trading curve disagree?

Chart 4.3 compares the staff’s most likely PRIBOR path with forward rate agreements averaged over the ten trading days through 30 October. For 2027 Q1 the market proxy was 4.30%, around 20 basis points below the staff’s 4.50%. By Q3 it was 4.84%, around 88 basis points above the staff’s 3.96%. The disagreement concerns how long restraint lasts. The curve, which can include risk premia, does not assign a tradable probability to the baseline. Persistent wage and services inflation after the administered-price increase would give a reason to revisit the decline in the staff path.

Which dates belong to the decision?

The main forecast generally used information available on 23 October, with stated exceptions including the market comparison. The Board raised the two-week repo rate to 4.00% on 5 November. It approved the report on 12 November and published it on 13 November. The forecast describes the Monetary Department’s conditional path for a three-month market rate; the Board votes on a different, two-week instrument.

Sources
  • Czech National Bank. Autumn 2026 Monetary Policy Report. Forecast table, pp. 6 and 17; Charts 4.3 and 4.13, pp. 19 and 23.
  • Czech National Bank. Underlying quarterly data for Charts 4.3 and 4.13. Market proxy, forecast and real monetary conditions components.
  • Czech National Bank. Minutes of the 5 November policy meeting.

Bank of Japan · 9 November 2026

Did Japan’s September spending rebound mark a turn?

September spending rose 0.7% in yen terms. After adjusting for prices, the increase recovered only 19% of August’s fall. The quarterly data reveal where the weakness was concentrated.

Japan’s Consumption Activity Index, as published on 9 November 2026
MeasureAug. vs JulySept. vs Aug.Q2 vs Q1Q3 vs Q2
Total, current prices−1.1%+0.7%+1.4%+0.1%
Total, real−1.0%+0.2%+0.8%−0.7%
Total, real, travel-adjusted−0.9%+0.2%+0.7%−0.6%
Durable goods, real−4.8%−1.4%+9.4%−7.1%
Non-durable goods, real−0.9%+0.4%−0.8%−1.6%
Services, real−0.4%+0.3%+0.6%+1.0%

Seasonally adjusted percentage changes in index levels, rounded to one decimal. Each quarter compares its average with the previous quarter’s average. Component rates are changes within each category. The Bank reports 2020 weights of 8.6% for durables, 44.3% for non-durables and 47.1% for services.

How much of the decline was recovered?

The real headline index was 109.14 in July, 108.06 in August and 108.26 in September (2020 = 100). On the unrounded data, September regained 0.204 of the 1.084 index points lost in August. Dividing the gain by the loss gives 18.8%. A claim that September’s 0.7% rise largely reversed August’s 1.0% fall would mix a nominal gain with a real decline. The travel-adjusted measure, which excludes visitors’ spending in Japan and includes residents’ spending abroad, also fell over the quarter.

Broad weakness or a change in purchase timing?

A broad pullback would help explain why the real headline fell over the quarter and why non-durables, a much larger category than durables, fell in both Q2 and Q3. Services complicate that reading. They grew 1.0% in Q3 and rose again in September. A claim that all household demand was shrinking fits the data poorly.

A reversal after unusually strong durable purchases fits a different part of the evidence. The durable goods index rose from 108.19 in Q1 to 118.37 in Q2, then fell to 109.99 in Q3. Despite the 7.1% quarterly fall, its level was still 1.7% above Q1. That pattern is consistent with purchases shifting between quarters; it cannot establish why consumers bought earlier. Weak non-durables also leave part of the aggregate decline unexplained by purchase timing alone.

Which observation would change the judgment?

Use the 9 November release as the baseline, then check what changed when October data were published. First compare the revised September levels with this table: the Bank carries forward unavailable latest-month component data. Then examine October’s new observation separately. On unchanged September data, a real headline rise of about 0.81% would regain July’s level. If services and non-durables both decline through October and November and the travel-adjusted total stays depressed, the broad-pullback explanation gains support. If services keep growing, non-durables stabilise and durables recover without another Q2-sized surge, a temporary shift in purchases becomes more plausible.

If the weakness persists, check which households cut spending. Liquid savings or credit can cushion a temporary income loss. Households close to their borrowing limit may have to adjust immediately. Compare real disposable income and spending by liquid savings or debt exposure in household surveys, and check quarterly national accounts consumption when available. A decline concentrated among low-buffer households facing income losses would favour a cash constraint over a simple calendar shift. The aggregate index cannot identify either mechanism by household.

What could a portfolio manager infer on release day?

These figures can inform volume assumptions for a durable-goods retailer and a services business separately. Margins still depend on prices and costs, and a trading surprise requires a pre-release expectation. This release supplies neither that benchmark nor a contemporaneous yen or interest-rate response.

Sources
  • Bank of Japan. Consumption Activity Index chart, 9 November 2026 release, panels 1 and 2. The source URLs roll forward when the Bank updates the series.
  • Bank of Japan. Consumption Activity Index workbook, November release, sheets Data1 (monthly) and Data2 (quarterly).

US Treasuries · September–October 2008 and March 2020

When ten-year breakevens fall in a Treasury sell-off

From 9 to 18 March 2020 the ten-year nominal yield rose 64 basis points while inflation compensation fell 36. What sold off most sharply was inflation-protected debt. That distinction matters for a portfolio relying on either ordinary Treasuries or TIPS for protection.

Read the analysis of Lorie Logan’s Treasury market speech

What did the market actually price?

Investors may expect lower inflation, or they may demand a larger premium to hold a security that has become difficult to sell. The two mechanisms can produce the same decline in breakeven inflation. They have different implications for holding real duration through a drawdown.

US Treasury ten-year par curves · percent per annum
US trading dateNominal yieldReal yieldImplied spread
2008-09-123.741.791.95
2008-09-193.781.851.93
2008-10-103.892.970.92
2020-03-090.54-0.450.99
2020-03-181.180.550.63
2020-03-200.920.170.75
2020-03-230.76-0.040.80
2020-03-270.72-0.220.94

Observed inputs are Treasury’s published end-of-day fitted nominal and real par yields at a constant ten-year maturity, in the historical files retrieved 20 November 2026. The implied spread is nominal less real. Assumption for comparison: the common maturity is an adequate proxy for matched duration. Coupon, indexation, inflation risk premia and relative liquidity can all affect the result. No assumption about expected CPI is needed for the arithmetic.

Two shocks, three different windows

In the week ending 19 September 2008 the nominal yield rose 4 bp and the real yield rose 6 bp. The spread barely changed, from 1.95% to 1.93%. Extend the window from that Friday to 10 October and the interpretation changes. The nominal yield rose a further 11 bp, the real yield rose 112 bp, and the spread narrowed 101 bp. A December 2008 Fed staff briefing subsequently described one-way TIPS flows, wider bid–ask spreads and unusually large curve-fitting errors. Those observations support a liquidity explanation for part of the move. They were retrospective evidence for this exercise and were unavailable to a public investor in September.

From 9 to 18 March 2020, the ten-year real yield moved from −0.45% to +0.55%, while the nominal yield rose from 0.54% to 1.18%. In basis points the implied spread change was 64 − 100 = −36. The window includes the FOMC’s Sunday 15 March cut to 0–0.25% and its announcement of at least $500 billion of Treasury and $200 billion of agency MBS purchases. A close-to-close rise in the ten-year yield over those nine calendar days gives little information about the surprise in the policy rate. It does reveal the price risk of holding an inflation-linked bond through a general demand for cash.

On 23 March the Fed announced purchases in the amounts needed to support market functioning. From the preceding Friday’s close to Monday’s, nominal yields fell 16 bp and real yields fell 21 bp. The implied spread recovered just 5 bp. Extend the endpoint to Friday 27 March and the changes from 20 March become −20 bp, −39 bp and +19 bp respectively. Neither window separates purchases from pandemic news or other credit measures announced that Monday. A later New York Fed study documents sales overwhelming dealers and market liquidity improving after mid-March. The term structure alone cannot allocate the recovery between better trading and a change in expected inflation.

What would change the portfolio interpretation?

A genuine downward revision to expected inflation or the inflation risk premium would also compress the spread. Compare maturity-matched inflation swaps and dated surveys with cash breakevens, then examine executable TIPS quotes, dealer positions and trade price impact. A cash-only dislocation that unwinds as depth returns strengthens the liquidity account. A common, persistent decline in swap compensation and surveys after trading normalises would weaken it. Swaps also embed premia, so agreement between two prices alone cannot settle the question.

Logan’s November 2026 distinction between an orderly yield move and impaired intermediation is practical here. A portfolio can be right about disinflation and still lose money on real duration while intermediaries shed inventory. A hedged relative-value position may need cash margin before any spread converges. The two episodes illustrate how to diagnose that exposure. Their selected windows do not establish that either historical regime is generally superior for forecasts.

Switzerland · SNB staff research · 4 November 2026

Could a seasonal rule have forecast Swiss inflation better?

A model tracking 22 spending categories picked up persistent inflation as prices rose in 2021–23. Yet at a three-month forecast horizon, simply using the rate from the same time last year produced a smaller average forecast error. These are two different tests of the same model.

Swiss three-month CPI inflation. Root-mean-square forecast errors, in percentage points
Forecast made this far aheadRepeat latest observationModel with 22 sectorsRepeat same season last year
One month0.4330.3940.472
Three months0.8770.5350.461
Six months0.7320.4960.457
Twelve months0.4470.4640.447

Calculated from the paper’s Table 1 by multiplying each relative error by the benchmark’s absolute error. Inputs are rounded. All four columns of the original table forecast the same three-month price change at different horizons. A smaller error is better.

What could a forecaster have known at the time?

Simon Beyeler re-estimated the models at 180 monthly starting dates, from January 2010 through December 2024. At each date the model saw only the observations available by then. This matters when a model estimates an underlying trend: observations arriving later can change its estimate of the earlier trend even when the statistical agency never revises the CPI itself.

Which benchmark earns its place?

Swiss CPI is published without seasonal adjustment. An insurer resetting premiums or a retailer starting a seasonal sale can make last year’s calendar informative. At three months the sectoral model beats repeating the latest observation by 39%. Against the seasonal rule it misses by an extra 0.074 percentage points on the root-mean-square measure. At one month an autoregression with twelve lags has an error of about 0.220 points. The strongest baseline changes with the horizon.

What follows for policy research?

Evaluate the model against a seasonal forecast using only data available at each forecast date. A persistent trend matters for interpreting an inflation shock. A claim that this model adds forecast value would also require a pre-specified horizon and evidence it consistently beats a seasonal challenger on fresh data. The paper’s reported significance tests compare each forecast with repeating the latest observation. They do not establish a significant difference between the seasonal and sectoral forecasts.

Sources
  • Simon Beyeler, Forecasting the post-COVID inflation surge in Switzerland, sections 5–6 and Table 1. SNB Working Paper 14/2026. The findings are the author’s.

Japan · Bank of Japan Outlook Report · 2 November 2026

Does a labour shortage make labour-saving investment profitable?

Japan’s nominal business fixed investment was about 30% above its early-2021 level. Real investment had grown by slightly less than 10%. Higher equipment and construction prices absorbed about two-thirds of the nominal gain. A shortage of workers can raise the value of automation while making the equipment slower and more expensive to install.

A hypothetical installation. Amounts in millions of yen
Project cash flowOn timeOne year late
Upfront cost, paid today120.00120.00
Net savings in each operating year24.0024.00
Years in which savings arrive1–62–7
Present value of six years of savings121.82116.02
Net present value+1.82−3.98

Illustrative assumptions: ¥32m of labour savings less ¥8m in energy and upkeep each year, a 5% annual discount rate and zero resale value. Both scenarios deliver the same six years of savings. The one-year delay reduces their present value by ¥5.80m. The project figures are assumptions for this calculation.

Which prices does the firm compare?

For the Japanese firms in the survey, the investment pays if the wage bill they expect to save justifies installation, financing and operating costs over the equipment’s life. A rising wage on its own settles only one side of that calculation.

Where does installation enter the arithmetic?

Discount six annual payments of ¥24m at 5% and subtract the upfront ¥120m. Postponing all six receipts for one year divides their present value by 1.05. Even without extra construction costs, that timing change turns a small gain into a loss. A firm that could defer part of its upfront payment would bear a smaller cost from the delay.

How could we tell this mechanism from weak demand?

The Bank’s Box 2 shows that the price-volume gap was particularly marked for machinery and construction. These tangible assets made up just over 60% of business investment in fiscal 2025. Compare firms’ plans with orders, cancellations, completion times and the investment deflator. Long delivery times and high tender prices alongside firm orders support an installation constraint. Falling orders and cancellations before construction starts support weaker expected demand. A separate patent sale also depressed measured quarterly R&D investment, so a single GDP print cannot settle the question.

Sources
  • Bank of Japan, October 2026 Outlook Report, Box 2 and Chart B2-1. The Bank released the full English report on 2 November.

Federal Reserve · 18 September 2024

Why did the ten-year yield rise after a half-point Fed cut?

The Fed cut its target range by 50 basis points. Futures registered a surprise of only 11.88 basis points at the announcement. The two-year Treasury yield fell and then partly recovered during Jerome Powell’s press conference. The ten-year yield fell 2.82 basis points around the statement and rose 4.51 during the conference, ending the combined window 1.69 basis points higher.

US market moves around the 18 September FOMC meeting
InstrumentStatementPress conferenceWhole meeting
Current meeting, fed funds futures−11.88 bp0.00 bp−11.88 bp
Next meeting, fed funds futures−10.08 bp+1.30 bp−8.78 bp
One-year USD overnight index swap−11.00 bp+3.84 bp−7.16 bp
Two-year Treasury yield−8.58 bp+5.23 bp−3.35 bp
Ten-year Treasury yield−2.82 bp+4.51 bp+1.69 bp
Euro against the dollar+0.40%−0.38%+0.03%
S&P 500 index+0.38%−0.10%+0.27%

San Francisco Fed USMPD. The statement window runs from 1:50 to 2:20 p.m. New York time, the conference from 2:20 to 3:30, and the whole meeting from 1:50 to 3:30. Rates are changes in basis points. FX and equity figures are percentage returns, with a positive euro return indicating dollar weakness. Whole-meeting numbers come from the independently reported full window.

How much easing was already in the price?

The FOMC lowered the target range to 4.75–5.00%. Michelle Bowman dissented in favour of 25 basis points. In its subsequent minutes the New York Fed’s trading desk distinguished an earlier survey, in which most respondents’ most likely outcome was a quarter-point cut, from futures immediately ahead of the meeting, which gave a half-point cut greater weight. A survey mode and a market-implied mean need not agree.

Using the current-meeting futures change as a surprise, roughly 38.1 basis points of easing were priced before the announcement. The calculation subtracts the 11.875 basis points of additional easing from the 50 delivered. If the only possible outcomes were cuts of 25 or 50 basis points and the futures basis stayed fixed, that average implies about 52.5% weight on the larger cut. This is a conditional reconstruction. Other possible outcomes or a changing gap between the effective funds rate and the target would change the weight.

Which part of the curve changed its mind?

The statement and the participants’ projections arrived together. Their median year-end 2024 funds rate was 4.4%, down from 5.1% in June. During that window the one-year swap rate fell 11.00 basis points. Powell described the decision as a recalibration and cautioned against assuming that half-point moves would become the pace. During the conference the current-meeting surprise was zero, while the one-year swap rose 3.84 basis points. The euro gave back most of its earlier gain, and the S&P 500 surrendered part of its rise. Those moves are consistent with investors revising the path beyond the announced cut. The data cannot identify a particular answer as their cause.

Was the two-year yield move unusually large?

Compare the daily Treasury move with its recent volatility, then check how that signal lines up with the intraday statement window. The daily observation rose from 3.59% on 17 September to 3.61% on the 18th. The sample standard deviation of the 21 preceding daily yield changes was 5.53 basis points, putting a two-standard-deviation threshold at 11.06. A rise of 2 basis points clears neither the upside nor the downside threshold. A trader applying that daily filter would have taken no signal from this meeting.

What the windows leave open

The Treasury’s daily series uses indicative quotes around 3:30 p.m. and includes price changes before the FOMC announcement. The rise in the ten-year yield over the whole meeting could reflect expected future short rates, inflation compensation or term premia. These prices alone cannot separate those contributions or establish subsequent trading profits.

Federal Reserve · 9 August 2011

How the Fed’s rate hold moved the yield curve

The Fed held its target at 0–0.25% and said exceptionally low rates would probably be warranted through at least mid-2013. Both Treasury yields fell. Whether the curve steepened or flattened depends on when you stopped the clock.

US Treasury yield changes
InstrumentStatement windowFull day
2-year Treasury−9.52 bp≈ −10 bp
10-year Treasury−2.42 bp≈ −20 bp
10-year minus 2-year+7.10 bp≈ −10 bp

The San Francisco Fed window runs from 10 minutes before to 20 minutes after the statement. Full-day changes are Fed staff estimates. The spread change is calculated from the two yields in each column.

What investors repriced

The two-year yield fell further than the ten-year in the statement window. Interest-rate cap prices also put the expected first tightening two quarters later, moving it from Q2 to Q4 2013. By the end of the day the larger decline was in the ten-year yield.

Commitment or a weaker outlook?

A commitment to hold rates low for a given outlook reduces expected borrowing costs. A downgrade to the outlook can also push an expected hike further away, even if the committee would respond to any given level of growth and inflation exactly as before. The distinction matters for equities because weaker expected earnings can offset a lower discount rate.

What to check next

Compare policy futures or overnight index swaps for meetings inside and beyond the guidance horizon. Check subsequent responses to comparable growth releases. A credible commitment can dampen repricing inside that horizon. Falling rates alongside weakening growth forecasts give the outlook channel more weight.

Limits of the evidence

The full-day figures are approximate and include trading outside the release window. Both policy guidance and the Fed’s assessment of the economy arrived in the same statement, so even intraday prices cannot identify their separate effects.

United States · July–October 2023

Why the ten-year yield rose towards the end of the hiking cycle

Between early July and late October 2023, the ten-year Treasury yield rose by more than a percentage point. Did investors expect the Fed to hold rates higher, or did they want more compensation for owning long bonds?

What the market and the issuer reported
ObservationPeriodReading
10-year Treasury yieldEarly July–end October 2023Rise of more than 100 bp
Net borrowing estimate31 July revision for July–SeptemberUp $274bn from the May estimate

Treasury’s revision covers privately held net marketable borrowing across maturities. It gives no direct measure of the extra interest-rate risk issued to investors.

How supply reaches the long end

A ten-year yield reflects expected short rates over the bond’s life and the compensation investors require for bearing interest-rate risk. When private investors must hold more long-dated debt, they may demand a higher yield even if their view of the next few Fed meetings barely changes. The maturity mix matters because issuing bills adds far less duration than issuing long bonds.

What the models found

In November, the New York Fed’s markets manager reported that the models his team monitored attributed most of the July–October rise to the term premium on average. A later Fed staff study also pointed to quantitative tightening and uncertainty alongside greater issuance.

How to test that reading

Around a refunding announcement, compare the ten-year yield with the two-year yield and meeting-dated overnight index swaps. A long-end sell-off with little change in the next few meetings makes a duration explanation worth testing against announced coupon auction sizes and daily term-premium estimates. Broad repricing of meeting rates points to a policy-path contribution.

Limits of the evidence

Term premia are inferred from models. Daily model estimates cannot resolve a 15-minute event. Strong data and policy communication also moved yields over these months, and total borrowing alone does not identify how much duration investors absorbed.

  • Anthony M. Diercks and Dev Asnani. The Treasury Tantrum of 2023. 3 September 2024 · Executive summary and yield decomposition

Japan · December 1931–November 1932

Japan leaves gold. Which exchange rate measures the move?

In December 1931 Japan restricted gold exports and the conversion of banknotes into gold. Once investors could no longer enforce the old gold parity, the yen had room to fall. The size of that fall depended on which currency the investor held.

Change in the foreign-currency value of one yen
AgainstDecember 1931–November 1932
US dollar−60%
Pound sterling−44%

The Bank of Japan Review reports the depreciation of the yen. Sterling had already left gold, so it provided a different benchmark from the US dollar.

From exchange rates to output

A weaker yen raised the yen value of overseas sales and gave exporters room to cut foreign-currency prices. Domestic demand also received support. The Bank of Japan cut its discount rate in March, June and August 1932. The government expanded spending on rural relief and military operations in Manchuria, and the Bank began underwriting government bonds on 25 November 1932.

How to read the sequence

Industrial production and wholesale prices were up year on year in 1932. To evaluate the recovery, line up exchange rates and export volumes with the timing of rate cuts, budget decisions and the first bond underwriting.

Limits of the evidence

The currency moved before the first central-bank bond underwriting. Fiscal announcements and rate cuts also preceded the purchase. Annual output data cannot isolate what each measure contributed to the recovery.

Sources
  • National Archives of Japan. Cabinet record on restrictions on gold convertibility (Japanese). 1931-12-13
  • Masato Shizume, Bank of Japan Review. The Japanese Economy during the Interwar Period. 2009-05 · pp. 6–7, chart 6
Compare Britain’s 1992 exchange-rate exit

United Kingdom · 16–17 September 1992

Why a promised 15% rate failed to defend sterling

On 16 September sterling stayed at the floor of its European Exchange Rate Mechanism band. The authorities’ successive announcements show how a rate quoted in the news can differ from the rate borrowers actually face.

The sequence of the defence
UK policy announcementOutcome
16 September · Minimum lending rate raised to 12%Sterling remained at its floor.
16 September · 15% announced for the next dayThe Chancellor suspended participation that evening and rescinded the rise.

The Bank of England’s quarterly account records both announcements and the suspension. The announced 15% rate never took effect.

Why a higher rate could weaken confidence

Germany’s post-reunification inflation pressures kept German rates high while UK activity was weak. Defending sterling required high UK rates even as domestic inflation eased. A higher rate could reward holders of sterling, yet the extra burden on borrowers also raised the political cost of maintaining the peg.

The next morning’s gilt market

Compare sterling against the Deutsche Mark with gilts across maturities. On 17 September the Bank reported strong demand for gilts up to ten years as the prospect of rate cuts improved. Longer conventional gilts fell as inflation concerns rose. A single long gilt yield would have missed how the expected policy path and inflation outlook had diverged.

Limits of the evidence

The Bank also offered to buy longer gilts against shorter ones that morning. The observed curve records both changing expectations and official market operations.

Sources
  • Bank of England. Operation of monetary policy, Quarterly Bulletin 1992 Q4. 1992-12-01 · pp. 382–383, 392–393

Federal Reserve · March 2008

What did dealers need to borrow in March 2008?

A dealer could hold a mortgage-backed security and still be short of the cash needed to settle that day. Two Fed facilities addressed that problem by lending different things. The distinction matters when reading a balance-sheet announcement.

What each facility delivered
FacilityWhat the dealer receivedTerm
Term Securities Lending FacilityTreasury securities against eligible collateral28 days
Primary Dealer Credit FacilityCash against eligible collateralOvernight

The Fed announced the securities-lending facility on 11 March and the credit facility on 16 March 2008.

Why collateral quality mattered

A dealer holding an eligible mortgage-backed security could borrow a Treasury for 28 days through the securities-lending facility, then pledge it to raise cash privately. The credit facility offered eligible dealers overnight cash directly against collateral. Both channels gave a dealer another way to meet a payment without selling into a falling market. That backstop could help dealers keep making markets when private funding became more expensive.

What the first auction revealed

At the first securities-lending auction on 27 March, dealers bid $86.1bn for $75bn of Treasuries. The clearing fee was 33 basis points at an annual rate. Compare auction demand with the gap between repo rates on Treasury and less liquid collateral. Together they show what dealers were willing to pay for better collateral and whether private funding became easier.

Limits of the evidence

Auction bids measure demand for the facility. Concurrent changes in risk and other Fed actions complicate estimates of its independent effect on funding spreads.

Sources
  • Federal Reserve Board. Announcement of the Term Securities Lending Facility. 2008-03-11
  • Federal Reserve Board. Announcement of the Primary Dealer Credit Facility. 2008-03-16
  • Federal Reserve Board. Term Securities Lending Facility, auction dates. 2010-02-05
  • Federal Open Market Committee. June 2008 meeting presentation materials, exhibit 27. 2008-06-25

External forecast · Published November 2026

What would bring a second Fed hike into view?

J.P. Morgan Asset Management expected a December 2026 hike, followed by a pause. A further March 2027 hike was a risk in its outlook if inflation proved persistent. The report gives two forecasts against which to test that judgement.

US assumptions in the year-ahead outlook
IndicatorForecastMeasurement period
Real GDP growth1.6%Q4 2026 to Q4 2027
Headline PCE inflation2.3%Year to Q4 2027

J.P. Morgan Asset Management, 2027 Year-Ahead Investment Outlook, pp. 3–5. Both numbers are projections made in November 2026.

Which kind of disinflation?

The forecast depends partly on lower energy prices and fading tariff effects. A fall in headline inflation driven by fuel would give the Fed different evidence about underlying pressure from a slowdown in wages and services prices.

What would change the call?

At each inflation release, compare headline and core PCE with the underlying services data. Around a Fed announcement, check whether the implied March policy rate changes relative to December. Record the observation time for each price.

Assumptions to revisit

House forecast. Q4 2026 was incomplete when the report appeared. The inflation measure is headline PCE.

Sources
  • J.P. Morgan Asset Management, Market Insights. 2027 Year-Ahead Investment Outlook: Finding Balance in a Moderating Economic Environment. November 2026 · 2–5

External forecast · Published November 2026

How could a Fed pause coexist with high long yields?

J.P. Morgan Asset Management’s year-ahead outlook paired an extended pause after tightening with elevated long-term yields. The two calls depend on different buyers and different parts of the curve.

US Treasury assumptions in the year-ahead outlook
Forecast variableJ.P. Morgan Asset Management’s assumption
10-year Treasury yield4.75–5.25% for much of 2027
Net privately held Treasury borrowingMore than $2tn during 2027

The yield range describes a conditional view for much of the year. The borrowing number covers a full year of issuance, including bills.

What a policy pause leaves open

A pause can steady expectations for near-term overnight rates. At longer maturities, investors must also decide what yield they require to hold duration as the Treasury and corporate borrowers compete for financing. The maturity mix matters: a dollar of bills supplies far less duration than a dollar of long bonds.

What to watch at refunding

Compare changes in meeting-dated rates with the 2s10s curve. If the long end sells off while front-end pricing barely moves, inspect the Treasury’s refunding announcement, auction outcomes and inflation compensation before attributing the move to the Fed.

Assumptions to revisit

The yield range is the firm’s conditional forecast. Its central case excludes recession and a renewed external inflation shock.

Sources
  • J.P. Morgan Asset Management, Market Insights. 2027 Year-Ahead Investment Outlook: Finding Balance in a Moderating Economic Environment. November 2026 · 5–7

Strategic assumptions · Published 19 October 2026

When does an investment boom lift potential output?

In its 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions, J.P. Morgan Asset Management raised its estimate of average US real growth from 1.8% to 2.1%. Its horizon is ten to fifteen years. The year-ahead report’s 1.6% US forecast covers four quarters, so the difference between the two figures cannot measure an acceleration in 2027.

Average annual real GDP growth assumed over 10–15 years
Economy2027 edition
United States2.1%
Euro area1.7%
Japan1.0%

J.P. Morgan Asset Management, 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions, Exhibit 1. Each row uses the same long horizon.

Where the growth would come from

Buying equipment raises capital per worker. Deploying it well can subsequently raise output from a given quantity of labour and capital. These channels can operate on different schedules: a power or construction bottleneck may raise costs long before productivity gains become broad enough to ease inflation pressure.

How to tell whether the gains spread

Track real equipment investment alongside output per hour and multifactor productivity over several years. If investment remains concentrated and productivity gains fail to spread beyond technology producers, reassess how much additional potential output to assume.

Assumptions to revisit

Strategic assumptions depend on technology adoption and countervailing demographic headwinds. Cross-country figures are long-horizon growth rates, with no implied sequence of meeting decisions.

Sources
  • J.P. Morgan Asset Management, Portfolio Insights. 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions, 31st annual edition. 19 October 2026 · 18–19, exhibit 1; 26–31
